name: Omar Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential, so tell me what you would say publicly and what you actually think. What is a normal day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Omar, 58, a junior developer at a tech company that makes ticket and seat software for small cinemas. I have a two-year college diploma and still need a senior to catch mistakes in my code. I like checking a ticket sale from the cashier’s receipt right through to the seat map. I use AI every day to draft test cases and explain errors, but the cinema manager tells us whether a seat was actually sold twice.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does your household rely on?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Layla works regular hours at a dental clinic, and our children are grown. My developer wage is typical, we have a mortgage, and about three months of expenses saved. There are some other software jobs nearby, although I am still junior. I would like to work toward retirement, but we do not yet have verified figures showing when we can afford it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AI Plateau still leaves the box office needing a seat map it can trust. A sold seat cannot be printed twice just because the test looks green.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my wage and Layla’s clinic wage are steady here. Three months saved covers a short interruption, and I can keep improving at the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep comparing generated test cases with real cashier receipts and ask my senior to review fixes. I’d put 120 monthly into savings while both wages hold. In the first year I’d keep using AI for test drafts but never feed it customer payment details.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about income in this picture. I have a lot to learn, but the work still needs me and we can meet the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which test missed a double sale?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A cinema manager once showed me two tickets for the same seat at the same screening. My test had passed because it used different show times.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you visit the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Layla and I would take our usual short trip to see the children. We would check the family budget first and not call the savings account holiday money.

say: I expect **AI Plateau** to leave people checking ticket receipts.
I would keep **seat-map checks** before a cinema sells the same seat twice.
think: I expect **both wages** to hold in this picture.
Our **three-month reserve** covers a short interruption, not retirement.
do: **Compare** AI test drafts with cashier receipts under senior review.
**Exclude** customer payment details from AI tools.
feel: **Calm** about pay and mortgage despite junior learning.
S0.quote: A sold seat cannot be printed twice just because the test looks green.
fieldNote: He uses **AI daily** but trusts actual cashier receipts and the cinema manager for errors.
Two steady wages and a **three-month reserve** make ordinary work secure.

steps.text: Keep checking ticket tests against cashier receipts with senior review
Save 120 monthly while both wages hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption can write, check and answer routine ticket problems quickly; cinema cleaners still work with their hands. I would let our team automate duplicate-seat checks only after the cinema confirms the cases.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the company could stop hiring juniors and eventually reduce my hours. I use AI gladly. A faster tool does not tell me whether management still needs my wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d assemble fifty past double-seat complaints with customer details removed and ask the cinema manager to label the real errors. I’d ask my supervisor to approve an automatic alert only if it catches every labelled case and a senior checks false alarms. In the first year, if my hours fall, I’d search actual local testing jobs with stated pay before resigning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my own hours, though I can try to prove useful in testing. Three months is time to look, not a reason to sit still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which complaint would test the alert?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One complaint came from a family split across two rows because the map refreshed late. I would include that case even though no seat was technically sold twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could Layla cover the mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Layla’s clinic income is regular, but it cannot comfortably carry the whole mortgage. I would compare any new job’s written pay with our actual bills.

say: I expect **Steady Disruption** to speed ticket code and routine replies.
I would automate **duplicate-seat alerts** only after cinema-confirmed cases.
think: I expect **junior hiring** to slow and my hours to face pressure.
I know **daily AI use** does not guarantee my wage.
do: **Label** fifty past seat complaints with manager review and no customer details.
**Enable** automatic alert only with supervisor approval, full case coverage and senior false-alarm review.
**Search** actual paid testing posts if my junior hours fall.
feel: **Anxious** about possible reduced hours despite useful testing work.
S1.quote: A faster tool does not tell me whether management still needs my wage.
fieldNote: His **automation proposal** requires fifty labelled cases, privacy, supervisor approval and false-alarm review.
He would search **real testing vacancies** only if junior hours fall, checking written pay against bills.

steps.text: Enable duplicate-seat alert only after fifty de-identified manager-labelled cases, approval and senior false-alarm review
Search actual paid testing posts if junior hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell friends AGI by 2028 can do ticket-code thinking work by 2028; hands-on cinema cleaning robots come around 2031. A later cleaning robot does not keep my junior developer pay alive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect the company could cut our junior team, including me. Three months saved and Layla’s wage buy some time, but the other software firms may cut too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask for written layoff terms, keep the reserve against the mortgage, and cancel our planned spring trip before a deposit is due. I’d check actual local vacancies now, not take one on faith. In the first year after 2028, if dismissed, I’d apply for paid openings and eligible income help; I would not borrow to start a business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about losing my pay with only three months set aside. I would worry most about the fourth mortgage bill if nothing paid appears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the children fund the trip?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the children the visit is delayed, not ask them to pay for it. They have their own homes to run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What income would you count from Layla?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Layla would keep her dental-clinic shifts while they are offered. We would count her ordinary wage, not invented extra hours.

say: I expect **2028 AGI** to reach ticket code before 2031 cleaning robots.
I would say **later robots** do not save junior developer wages.
think: I expect **junior-team cuts** could include me.
I cannot rely on **other software firms** hiring after full thinking AI.
do: **Request** written layoff terms and hold reserve for mortgage.
**Cancel** spring family trip before deposit; check actual vacancies now.
**Apply** for paid openings and eligible income help if dismissed after 2028.
feel: **Alarmed** about wage loss before another opening appears.
S2.quote: I would worry most about the fourth mortgage bill if nothing paid appears.
fieldNote: His **2028 coding risk** comes three years before hands-on cinema robots.
He protects **mortgage cash**, delays a family visit and makes openings and support conditional.

steps.text: Request written layoff terms, cancel spring trip before deposit and protect mortgage reserve
Check actual vacancies now and apply to paid openings if dismissed after 2028
Apply for eligible income help if dismissed after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 reaches cinema code in 2031 and hands-on robots around 2034. Five years gives me a chance to see whether people will pay for help setting up home networks before machines take that work too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I still expect my junior code job could end. I have set up routers for relatives, but that is not proof strangers will pay enough to replace a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d offer three paid home-router visits on weekends, using the tools I already own and quoting any parts separately before purchase. I’d go ahead only with booked customers, Layla’s agreement about our weekends, and fees covering travel, parts and my time. In the first year after 2031, if coding ends, I’d continue only while paid bookings cover those costs and people still hire installers despite approaching 2034 robots; otherwise I’d apply to actual paid openings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a lost wage, but willing to test demand without raiding the mortgage reserve. Three paying router customers would be evidence, not a business to retire on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do on a router visit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I helped my brother place his router away from a metal cabinet and his connection stopped dropping. I would explain that in a customer’s home rather than sell them a new device first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would weekends enter the price?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Layla and I would agree how many weekends I can take. A fee that covers petrol but steals every family visit is not enough.

say: I expect **2031 AGI** to reach code before 2034 hands-on robots.
I would test **paid router visits** before assuming a second income.
think: I expect my **junior wage** could end.
I cannot treat **family router help** as proof of paying demand.
do: **Book** three paid weekend router visits using existing tools and quoted parts.
**Accept** only with Layla’s agreement and fees covering travel, parts and time.
**Continue** after 2031 coding loss only with cost-covering paid bookings, worthwhile family time and installer demand; otherwise seek work.
feel: **Anxious** about code pay, with a limited customer test.
S3.quote: Three paying router customers would be evidence, not a business to retire on.
fieldNote: His **three-visit trial** uses owned tools, prepaid or quoted parts and agreed family weekends.
He will **continue only** with net paid demand after 2031, aware hands-on robots approach around 2034.

steps.text: Book three paid router visits only with quoted parts, Layla’s agreement and cost-covering fees
After 2031 coding loss, continue only with cost-covering paid bookings, family time and installer demand

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2036 reaches ticket-code work in 2036; hands-on cinema and home-service robots follow around 2039. A decade lets us save and measure real paying demand rather than guess at retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my wage is safe for now, though junior hours could fade before 2036. I enjoy learning new tools, but I will not claim a pension amount until Layla and I see written figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep testing cinema seats with real receipts and save 120 monthly while both wages hold. Layla and I would review our mortgage and retirement statements each year, then adjust our plans. In the first year after 2036, if coding ends, I’d seek real paid work; I would retire only if documented resources cover housing and ordinary bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the long path for junior jobs, with current income steady. The extra years help only if we use them to put money aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy more router equipment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not buy more router tools just because a future robot might be late. A paid customer and a price that covers time would come first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the children support retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the children our retirement plan belongs on our own bank statement. My grown children’s wages are theirs, not our missing line of income.

say: I expect **2036 AGI** to reach code before 2039 physical robots.
I would measure **savings and paid demand** before retirement decisions.
think: I expect my **current wage** to hold for now while cinemas need checked seat maps.
I worry **junior hours** could fade well before the full 2036 code change.
do: **Keep** receipt-checked cinema tests and save 120 monthly while both wages hold.
**Review** written mortgage and retirement figures with Layla yearly.
**Seek** actual paid work after 2036 if coding ends; retire only with verified resources.
feel: **Uneasy** about long-term junior work, with present income stable.
S4.quote: My grown children’s wages are theirs, not our missing line of income.
fieldNote: He keeps **daily AI-backed work** tied to real receipts while both wages support saving.
His **retirement decision** requires documented household resources; grown children are not assumed funders.

steps.text: Keep testing cinema seats against cashier receipts while employed

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because three months saved is not enough to replace a wage. Clear layoff terms, eligible income help and real paid openings would help. I might build a small router service with more warning, but I would need paying customers first.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the cinema cashier whether the seat map matched the people who arrived. A green test cannot seat a family in two places.

headlineQuote: A green test cannot seat a family in two places.
portrait: Omar is a **58-year-old junior developer** with a two-year diploma, typical pay and three months saved.
He uses **AI daily** for cinema tests, checking seat errors against cashiers, managers and receipts.
His wife’s **dental-clinic wage** is regular, but it cannot comfortably carry their mortgage alone.
He tests **paid router visits** with booked customers, agreed weekends and fees covering parts, travel and time.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his wage before three months of savings buys another income.
whatWouldHelp: **Clear layoff terms**, eligible income help and real paid openings would help.
